faq.q: Why do excitement and nerves feel the same?
faq.a: Both switch on the same body system: adrenaline makes your heart beat faster and your tummy flutter. Your brain decides what to call it based on what you are thinking.
asks: Are nerves and excitement the same thing?

faq.q: How do I turn nerves into excitement?
faq.a: Notice the fast heart and butterflies, then say, "I am excited!" Think about what could go well. Your body stays ready for action, but the feeling becomes more helpful.
asks: How do I stop being nervous before a show?

faq.q: Is it bad to feel nervous before a performance?
faq.a: No. Nearly everyone feels nervous before something important, even famous performers. A bit of nervous energy can help you focus and do your best.
asks: Do famous people get stage fright?

faq.q: What if my nerves are too strong?
faq.a: Try slow belly breathing and remind yourself the feeling will pass. If nerves are so strong that you avoid things you want to do, talk to a trusted grown-up or a school counsellor.

faq.q: Why do I feel sick before something exciting?
faq.a: When you are keyed up, your body sends blood away from your tummy to your muscles. That can make your tummy feel funny or a bit sick. It fades once you get going.
asks: Why do I feel sick before a race?

facts: In a 2014 study at Harvard Business School, people who told themselves "I am excited" before singing, public speaking or a maths test performed better than those who tried to calm down.
Excitement and nervousness both involve adrenaline, which raises your heart rate.
